newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wrestles with chemical treaty ratification.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wrestles with chemical treaty ratification.

text.p: A fierce battle over an international treaty outlawing chemical weapons resumes in the U.S. Senate this week as President Bill Clinton mounts an all-out campaign for a favourable vote on it this month.

The Foreign Relations Committee, headed by treaty foe Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican, opens new hearings on the pact on Tuesday with a barrage of opposition by three former defence secretaries.
Their well-honed arguments will be heard more than four years after 130 countries signed the treaty.

Administration officials are saying time is running out. The treaty comes into force on April 29 -- 180 days after the 65th country ratified it -- and unless the United States signs up by then, it will have no say in its administration.
The treaty bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons.

Clinton, leading a White House rally on Friday with an array of public figures supporting the pact including prominent Republicans, linked ratification to "whether we will continue to make America's leadership strong and sure."

Referring to lengthy negotiations between senior officials and key senators aimed at moving the treaty to the Senate floor, Clinton said the administration had "gone the extra mile" to meet senators' concerns.
Helms in a later statement made clear the administration had not gone far enough, accusing it of stone-walling.

Before the Senate can vote -- treaty approval requires a two-thirds majority by that house -- the pact must be cleared by Helms's committee, and Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott, a treaty critic, must schedule it for action.
Senate Democrats, seeking to put put pressure on Lott, have threatened to hold up all Senate action unless the treaty is brought up for debate.

Lott has indicated willingness to do so and Helms, at a joint news conference with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in his home state last month, also said he may be willing to allow the treaty to come to a vote.

But in his announcement of the upcoming hearings, Helms on Friday accused the administration of stonewalling on negotiations to address concerns on the treaty and said "their opposition to making essential changes will ensure the Senate never ratifies the Chemical Warfare Convention."
However a Senate Democratic aide insisted the negotiations had been "constructive".

Both sides of the debate have heavyweight allies. Joining former Secretary of State James Baker at the White House on Friday were retired Gen. Colin Powell and other members of the Joint Chiefs of Staff he once led. Many other military leaders have endorsed the treaty.

Opponents include four former defence secretaries, among them Dick Cheney, who served under President George Bush. Former secretaries Caspar Weinberger, Donald Rumsfeld and James Schlesinger testify at the Foreign Relations hearing on Tuesday. They will be followed on Wednesday by former U.N. Amassador Jeane Kirkpatrick and others opposed to the treaty.
Critics say the treaty cannot be verified against cheating and "rogue" statues like Libya and Iran will not honour it.

They also say treaty regulations would burden manufacturers and required inspections would invite industrial spying and could be unconstitutional. They say chemicals such as teargas would be outlawed.
Treaty supporters stress that the United States is already committed to destroying its poison gas stocks and say the pact is adequately verifiable.
The supporters include the Chemical Manufacturers Association, which says failure to ratify would hurt American chemical firms because the treaty imposes sanctions on non-participant countries.

The Foreign Relations hearings will be a replay. The committee previously approved the pact and sent it to the Senate last April. But at the administration's request the Senate shelved it in September after a letter of opposition from Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole threatened to make it a victim of election-year politics.
